extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Doctrines governing implied licenses (sales, employer/employee, partnership, estoppel) and legal standards for obtaining extensions of letters-patent, including who may obtain extensions and the evidentiary/quantitative showing required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of patented article conveys implied license to use that specific article
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee sells his patented instrument or machine for use by others ... the right to use passes by the sale; the purchaser obtains the right, by implication, to use or sell the specific article after the patent has been granted, with the same freedom from restrictions as if he had bought it from the patentee during the existence of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal rule: a sale by the patentee vests in the purchaser the right to use the particular article sold (‘‘the right to use passes by the sale’’). Where the patentee finds his remuneration in the sale of manufactured products, recovery against an infringer that adopts the sale may be treated as adopting the sale and thus vests the right to use the specific articles for which recovery is had. Examples/cases: Spaulding v. Page; Gilbert & Barker Mfg. Co. v. Bussing; Steam Stone Cutter Co. v. Sheldon. Limitations: the license is to the specific articles sold (use ‘‘so long as it lasts’’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of judgment and satisfaction on implied license to purchaser
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere judgment against an infringing seller, without satisfaction, does not confer an implied license on the purchaser; satisfaction of the judgment (i.e., payment) may create an implied license in the buyer to use the specific articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judgment is satisfied (paid), the buyer may have an implied license to use; if not satisfied the purchaser cannot use the device without the patentee's consent. Nominal damages or mere recovery of nominal damages do not create an implied license. Cases: Tuttle v. Matthews; Fisher v. Consolidated Amador Mine; Birdsell v. Shaliol; decisions cited in discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license from permission to make before patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, before his application for a patent, the inventor sells the article which is to be protected or knowingly permits another to construct it without a contract limiting its use, the purchaser or maker obtains the right, by implication, to use or sell the specific article after the patent is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope: the implied right covers the specific thing made or sold before the application; under statutes (cited Rev. Stat. Sec. 4899) the right is confined to that specific article. Cases: Brickill v. City of New York; other authorities cited. Practical note: absence of a limiting contract at time of transfer is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer has no automatic ownership but may obtain an implied license to use employee inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer, simply as such, has no right to the inventions of his employee. But where an employee uses the time, tools, or money of the employer and applies the invention in the employer's business, law implies a license to the employer to continue use even after employment ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ownership vs license: a prior contract for inventive skill or an express agreement may make employer equitable owner; absent that, implied license arises from circumstances (use of employer's tools/time, experiments at employer's expense, incorporation into employer's machines). Duration depends on nature of invention: if an art/process the employer may practise it for the patent term; if an article/machine only the specific machines made are licensed (use until worn out and repair while identity retained). The implied license is personal to the employer and not assignable like a purchaser's license. Cases: Wade v. Metcalf; McClurg v. Kingsland; Chabot v. American Button-hole; Barry v. Crane Bros.; Jencks v. Langdon Mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of employment contract or assignment on employer rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If the employer contracts for the employee's inventive skill and pays for it, he may become the equitable owner of resulting inventions and be entitled to assignments of patents; a contract for exclusive rights for a given period carries corresponding exclusive license rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is an express agreement (e.g., hired to invent, paid for inventive skill, or a prior contract assigning inventions), the employer's rights are governed by that agreement and may include ownership or an exclusive license covering all patents and extensions during the period contracted. Cases: Joliet Mfg. Co. v. Dice; Wilkens v. Spafford; Time Telegraph Co. v. Himmer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license rules for inventions developed in the firm/partnership or by corporate members
rubrics_metrics.description: If a co-partner or a corporate member makes an invention at the cost of the firm or applies it to the common business, the right to use vests in the partnership or corporation; on dissolution rights in specific articles may pass to members who received them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license in favor of the firm is implied when invention made at firm expense for common benefit; on dissolution the license may terminate, but specific constructed articles distributed among members carry the right to use as if the partnership continued. Similar rules apply to corporations whose members permit use by the corporation. Cases: Wade v. Metcalf; Montross v. Mabie; Brickill v. Mayor of New York.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied licenses arising by estoppel: requisites and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An implied license may arise out of any circumstances which operate as an estoppel on the patent owner to deny rights to the apparent licensee, but such circumstances must be unequivocal and amount to a complete and perpetual release of the specific articles from the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key limits/anti-patterns: mere acquiescence in known infringements does not authorize their continuance; a judgment for past infringements does not license future use; a use under a defective patent or failure to sue does not ipso facto create a license. Positive conduct that induces the user to place himself in a position of reliance such that he must suffer injury unless use is conceded may create an implied license by estoppel. Interpretation: courts construe implied licenses according to the legal rules under which they arise and the evident intention of the parties. Cases: Gear v. Grosvenor; Montross v. Mabie; cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and beneficiary of patent extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole object of an extension is to furnish to an inventor an additional opportunity to secure the recompense which he has hitherto failed to obtain; no extension will be granted unless the inventor is to enjoy at least a substantial portion of its benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences: extensions are granted for the inventor's benefit — if assignees or others are to reap the benefit without reasonable consideration to inventor, extension may be refused. The inventor need not hold legal title if he retains a reasonable beneficial interest; where there is no contract to assign the extension the inventor is presumed to have the beneficial interest. Joint patents require all joint inventors to desire extension; executor/administrator may apply and will hold in trust for heirs/assignees. Cases and Ex parte decisions cited (e.g., Ex parte Baker, Ex parte Munger, Ex parte Cox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and evidentiary showing required for patent extension (value and inadequate remuneration)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor is entitled to an extension only when the recompense received during the original term is not commensurate with the benefit conferred; the value of the invention must be demonstrated by experience or by the nature of the process or instrument and not rest in conjecture or mere assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden: applicant must prove practical value in the arts and actual profit (or lack thereof) derived; improvements made since issuance cannot be the sole basis for value claimed; sufficiency of remuneration already obtained is a question of fact for each case. Practical negatives: patents in little demand or gone out of use will not be extended; evidence such as a contract to purchase for a substantial sum may demonstrate value. Cases/Ex parte decisions cited: Ex parte Lockwood; Ex parte Marston; Ex parte Roots; Ex parte Slemmons; Ex parte Behr.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements and limitations on extension applications (who may apply, interest disclosure, and reissue effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise relation of the inventor to the patent must appear on the face of his application for extension; if less than the whole future benefit is to be enjoyed by him the precise proportion must be specifically stated. Where a patent has been reissued with the assignee's involvement, extension availability may depend on whether the inventor consented to the reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules/examples: where assignees reissued without inventor concurrence, extension may be based on original or reissued patent; but if inventor consented to reissue only the reissue may be extended. A joint patent generally requires all joint inventors to desire extension (one may apply if others later ratify). Executors/administrators holding on trust may apply. If applicant has parted with part of his interest, the application must clearly show what interest remains. Cases/Ex parte citations: Ex parte Low; Ex parte Dickinson; Ex parte Beadle; Ex parte Lee; Ex parte Packer.
